objectives: Distinguish a population (size $N$) from a sample (size $n$), and descriptive from inferential statistics.
Classify a variable as quantitative or categorical, even when categories are coded with numbers.
Compute relative and cumulative relative frequencies from counts.
Choose and read bar graphs, pie charts, dotplots, stem-and-leaf plots, histograms, and ogives.
recognize: Labels or groups (country, blood type, ZIP code) → counts and relative frequencies; bar graph or pie chart.
Numerical measurements → dotplot, stem-and-leaf plot, or histogram with left-closed classes $[a,b)$.
“What fraction is at or below this boundary?” → cumulative relative frequency / ogive.
mistakes: Treating numeric codes for categories as quantitative data.
Putting a boundary value in the wrong class: $[0.02,0.03)$ excludes 0.03.
Reading ogive height as a density or as the probability of one value.
Comparing raw-frequency bar heights when histogram classes have unequal widths.

objectives: Compute the mean, median, mode, and range of a dataset.
Compute sample variance and standard deviation with the $n-1$ divisor, by definition and by the computational formula.
Explain why the median is resistant and the mean is not.
State the units of each summary and keep sample and population notation separate.
recognize: Skewed data or an extreme value → report the median as a resistant center.
“Sample variance / sample standard deviation” → divide squared deviations by $n-1$.
An entire finite population → $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ with divisor $N$.
mistakes: Finding the median without sorting first.
Dividing a sample variance by $n$ instead of $n-1$.
Reporting the variance when the standard deviation is requested (or vice versa).
Rounding $\bar x$ early when using the computational formula, which can magnify error.

objectives: Compute and interpret z-scores; convert back with $x=\bar x + z s$.
Find quartiles with the course convention: for odd $n$, include the median in both halves.
Compute IQR, inner and outer fences, and classify mild and extreme outliers using the inclusive rule.
Draw a boxplot (whiskers to the most extreme non-outliers) and give the five-number summary (actual min and max).
recognize: “How unusual is this value?” or comparing positions on different scales → z-scores.
“Is this an outlier?” or “draw a boxplot” → quartiles, IQR, and fences.
A value exactly on a fence → the course counts it as an outlier (inclusive rule).

key_formulas.label: z-score
key_formulas.tex: z_i = \frac{x_i - \bar x}{s},\qquad x_i = \bar x + z_i s

mistakes: Using a calculator or software quartile convention instead of the course convention.
Treating a value exactly on a fence as not an outlier (strict inequality).
Drawing whiskers to the fences instead of to the most extreme non-outlying observations.
Putting whisker endpoints in the five-number summary instead of the actual minimum and maximum.

objectives: Write sample spaces and events as sets.
Use union, intersection, complement, and De Morgan's laws to translate verbal events.
Apply $P(A)=\#A/\#S$ only when elementary outcomes are equally likely.
Distinguish mutually exclusive events from other relationships.
recognize: “At least one …” → work with the complement “none”.
“Neither …” or “not both …” → De Morgan's laws.
Dice, coins, cards with physical symmetry → count equally likely ordered outcomes.

key_formulas.label: De Morgan
key_formulas.tex: (A\cup B)^c = A^c\cap B^c,\qquad (A\cap B)^c = A^c\cup B^c

mistakes: Counting outcomes that are not equally likely (e.g. the 11 dice sums).
Taking the complement of “both occur” to be “neither occurs”.
Assuming probability zero always means impossible (true for finite equally likely models, not in general).
Calling a collection mutually exclusive when only some pairs are disjoint.

objectives: Apply the multiplication rule to multistage choices.
Decide between permutations and combinations by asking whether order matters.
Count arrangements of objects with repeated types.
Build probabilities as ratios of counts with a consistent ordering convention.
recognize: Roles, rankings, or arrangements → order matters → $_nP_k$.
Committees, hands, subsets → order does not matter → $\binom nk$.
Letters of a word with repeats → $n!/(n_1!\cdots n_r!)$.
Repetition allowed (codes, passwords) → product $n^k$.
mistakes: Counting ordered outcomes in the numerator but unordered ones in the denominator.
Forgetting to divide by the factorials of repeated letters.
Using combinations when positions or roles are distinct.
Applying the multiplication rule when the number of options depends on earlier choices.

objectives: Use the probability axioms and the complement rule.
Apply the addition rule for two and three events.
Compute conditional probabilities and use the multiplication rule for sequential draws.
Test independence with $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ and distinguish it from disjointness.
recognize: “Given”, “if”, “among those who …” → conditional probability.
“A or B” → addition rule; subtract the overlap unless the events are disjoint.
Sequential draws without replacement → multiply conditional probabilities.
Physically separate mechanisms or stated independence → multiply unconditional probabilities.

key_formulas.label: Addition rule
key_formulas.tex: P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B)

mistakes: Confusing $P(A\mid B)$ with $P(B\mid A)$.
Believing disjoint events with positive probability are independent.
Multiplying probabilities without an independence or conditioning justification.
Forgetting the second order when “one of each” can happen in two orders.

objectives: Define a discrete random variable, its support, and its PMF.
Build a CDF and use $F(b)-F(a-1)$ for integer-valued variables.
Compute $E[X]$, $E[h(X)]$, $E[X^2]$, and $V(X)$.
Use linearity of expectation and the geometric-series sums from the notes.
recognize: A table of values with probabilities → PMF; expected value is a probability-weighted average.
“At most”, “at least”, “between” for integer values → CDF differences with careful endpoints.
A function of $X$ (cost, square, payoff) → $E[h(X)]=\sum h(x)p(x)$.
mistakes: Using $F(b)-F(a)$, which drops the value $a$.
Writing $E[X^2] = (E[X])^2$.
Not checking that a PMF is nonnegative and sums to 1.
Expecting $E[X]$ to be a possible value of $X$.

objectives: Specify a discrete uniform distribution by its actual support.
Model the number of trials through the first success as $G(p)$ (total trials, support $1,2,\ldots$).
Compute point and tail probabilities $P(X>k)$ and $P(X\ge k)$.
Use $E[X]=1/p$ and the standard deviation $\sqrt{1-p}/p$.
recognize: A finite list of values with equal probabilities → discrete uniform.
Repeat independent identical trials until the first success and count trials → geometric.
“More than $k$ trials needed” → the first $k$ trials all fail.
mistakes: Using a software geometric that counts failures (support from 0) without adding 1.
Off-by-one errors between $P(X>k)$ and $P(X\ge k)$.
Using geometric when trials are dependent or $p$ changes between trials.
Writing $U(k)$ without stating which $k$ values are possible.

objectives: Check the binomial conditions: fixed $n$, independent trials, constant $p$, count successes.
Compute binomial probabilities directly and from cumulative tables.
Model the number of trials until the $r$th success as negative binomial.
Explain the coefficient $\binom{x-1}{r-1}$ in the negative-binomial PMF.
recognize: Fixed number of independent trials, count the successes → $B(n,p)$.
Fixed number of successes, count the trials needed → $NB(r,p)$.
“The $r$th success occurs on trial $x$” → the last trial is a success.
mistakes: Using $\binom xr$ for a stopping-time event (it includes sequences that finished earlier).
Using the binomial for sampling without replacement from a small population.
Off-by-one table subtraction: $P(X\ge k) = 1-F(k-1)$, not $1-F(k)$.
Mixing up which outcome is labelled “success”.

objectives: Set up $HG(N,M,n)$ for sampling without replacement from a two-type population.
Compute probabilities with combinations and identify the feasible support.
Use $E[X]=nM/N$.
Explain why the binomial model does not apply exactly without replacement.
recognize: A finite population with two types, a sample drawn without replacement, count one type.
Cards from one deck, defective items in a lot, coloured tokens drawn from a box.
mistakes: Using $B(n, M/N)$ when draws are dependent and no approximation is justified.
Swapping the roles of $N$, $M$, and $n$.
Treating $M$ as a probability rather than a count.
Assigning probability to impossible values of $x$.

objectives: Use the Poisson PMF and interpret $\lambda$ as the expected count in the interval studied.
Use $E[X]=V(X)=\lambda$ and $sd=\sqrt\lambda$.
Scale a process rate to an interval: $\lambda = a t$ with matching units.
Distinguish a Poisson count from an exponential waiting time.
recognize: Counts of events over time, area, or volume at a stable average rate → Poisson.
“No events in time $t$” → $P(X=0)=e^{-at}$.
A bounded count from a fixed number of trials is binomial, not Poisson.
mistakes: Forgetting to convert the interval into the rate's time units.
Reporting $\lambda$ as the standard deviation.
Using Poisson for a count with a fixed maximum number of trials.
Confusing the event count with the waiting time between events.

objectives: State the PDF conditions and interpret probability as area under the density.
Construct a piecewise CDF, including values 0 and 1 outside the support.
Compute $E[X]$, $E[X^2]$, and $V(X)$ by integration.
Work with the continuous uniform $U(a,b)$.
recognize: A measurement on a continuum with a density formula → integrate over the event.
A CDF is given → subtract CDF values; differentiate to recover the density.
Equal density on an interval → continuous uniform; probabilities are length ratios.
mistakes: Treating $f(a)$ as $P(X=a)$; for continuous $X$, $P(X=a)=0$.
Ignoring the support when setting integration limits.
Leaving the CDF undefined outside the support instead of 0 below and 1 above.
Integrating $f(x)$ instead of $x f(x)$ to find a mean.

objectives: Use the gamma function and $\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!$.
Work with $\Gamma(\alpha,\beta)$ using the course's shape-scale convention.
Use the exponential $E(\beta)=\Gamma(1,\beta)$, its tail $P(X>t)=e^{-t/\beta}$, and link it to Poisson processes.
Identify $\chi^2_\nu$ as $\Gamma(\nu/2,2)$.
recognize: Waiting time to the first event of a Poisson process at rate $a$ → exponential with scale $\beta=1/a$.
An integral of the form $\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}e^{-x/\beta}dx$ → gamma function / gamma density kernel.
“Chi-squared with $\nu$ degrees of freedom” → $\Gamma(\nu/2,2)$.
mistakes: Reading $\beta$ as a rate instead of a scale.
Writing the variance as $\alpha\beta$ instead of $\alpha\beta^2$.
Writing $\Gamma(n) = n!$.
Forgetting that the density is zero for $x\le 0$.

objectives: Read $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with variance as the second parameter.
Standardize and use $\Phi$ for left tails, right tails, and intervals.
Find percentiles with $x_q=\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(q)$.
Distinguish Chebyshev's guaranteed lower bound from the normal empirical rule.
recognize: A normal model is stated → standardize with $\sigma$, then use $\Phi$.
“What value cuts off the top/bottom …%?” → inverse problem (percentile).
Distribution shape unknown, “at least what fraction?” → Chebyshev.
Approximately normal data and 1, 2, 3 standard deviations → empirical rule.
mistakes: Dividing by the variance instead of the standard deviation.
Reading the second parameter of $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ as $\sigma$.
Forgetting “1 −” for a right-tail probability.
Treating Chebyshev's bound as an exact probability, or 99.7% as a universal rule.

objectives: Define the moment-generating function $m_X(t)=E[e^{tX}]$ and its domain.
Obtain raw moments by differentiating at $t=0$, and variance from them.
Derive the MGF of the exponential density $e^{-x}$.
Reproduce the proof patterns in the notes: geometric sums, variance identity, gamma recurrence, unbiased $S^2$.
recognize: An MGF is given and a moment is requested → differentiate and evaluate at $t=0$.
“Show that …” about expectations → expand, then apply linearity and total probability one.
mistakes: Reporting $m''(0)$ as the variance.
Ignoring where the MGF exists (e.g. $t<1$).
Differentiating but forgetting to evaluate at $t=0$.
Skipping the boundary-term check in integration by parts.

objectives: Read a joint PMF table and check that it is valid.
Compute marginal distributions by summing out the other variable.
Compute event probabilities by summing the relevant cells.
Test independence by checking factorization in every cell; recognize the role of support for joint densities.
recognize: Two variables measured on the same unit with a table of probabilities → joint PMF.
“$P(X=x)$” from a joint table → row (or column) total.
“Are $X$ and $Y$ independent?” → compare $p(x,y)$ with $p_X(x)p_Y(y)$.
mistakes: Summing in the wrong direction when computing a marginal.
Concluding independence from one matching cell.
Assuming a constant joint density implies independence on a non-rectangular support.
Forgetting that all cells must sum to 1.

objectives: Compute $E[h(X,Y)]$ from a joint distribution.
Compute covariance with the shortcut $E[XY]-E[X]E[Y]$ and interpret its sign.
Compute correlation and use $-1\le\rho\le1$.
Apply the scaling rules and explain why zero covariance does not imply independence.
recognize: “Do $X$ and $Y$ tend to move together linearly?” → covariance or correlation.
A change of units or a linear transformation → $\operatorname{Cov}(aX+b,cY+d)=ac\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$.
Variance of a sum of dependent variables → include covariance terms.
mistakes: Concluding independence from zero covariance.
Thinking that adding a constant changes covariance.
Giving correlation units (it has none) or claiming covariance is unit-free.
Forgetting the absolute value: $sd(aX)=|a|\,sd(X)$.

objectives: Compute the sample correlation $R$ from paired data or z-scores.
Compute the least-squares slope and intercept from summary statistics.
Interpret slope, intercept, and $R^2$ in context.
State the limits: linear association only, no causation, care with extrapolation.
recognize: Paired quantitative data → scatterplot first, then $R$ and the least-squares line.
Given $\bar x,\bar y,s_x,s_y,R$ → slope $b=R\,s_y/s_x$, intercept $a=\bar y-b\bar x$.
“Percent of variation explained” → $R^2$ (as a percent if asked).

key_formulas.label: Slope and intercept
key_formulas.tex: b = R\frac{s_y}{s_x},\qquad a = \bar y - b\bar x

mistakes: Swapping $s_x$ and $s_y$ in the slope.
Expecting $R^2$ to keep the sign of the relationship.
Interpreting association as causation.
Extrapolating far beyond the observed $x$ values; concluding “no relationship” from $R\approx0$ when the pattern is curved.

objectives: Distinguish a parameter, an estimator (random), and an estimate (a number).
Compute bias and decide whether an estimator is unbiased.
Use $E[\bar X]=\mu$, $V(\bar X)=\sigma^2/n$, and $SE(\bar X)=\sigma/\sqrt n$.
Explain why $S^2$ divides by $n-1$ and why $S$ is generally biased.
recognize: “Is this estimator unbiased?” → compute $E[\hat\theta]-\theta$.
“How precise is the sample mean?” → standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$.
“How large a sample to cut the standard error by a factor $c$?” → multiply $n$ by $c^2$.
mistakes: Using $\sigma$ (spread of individuals) where $\sigma/\sqrt n$ (spread of the mean) is needed.
Dividing by $n$ and calling the result unbiased for $\sigma^2$.
Concluding $E[S]=\sigma$ from $E[S^2]=\sigma^2$.
Thinking “unbiased” means every estimate equals the parameter.

objectives: Compute the mean and variance of a linear combination $\sum a_iX_i$.
Use independence to drop covariance terms; square coefficients in variances.
State that a linear combination of independent normals is normal.
Use $\bar X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2/n)$ for IID normal samples, and distinguish an individual from a mean.
recognize: A total, difference, or weighted sum of independent normal variables → normal with summed mean and variance.
A probability about a sample mean → standardize with $\sigma/\sqrt n$, not $\sigma$.
A difference $X-Y$ of independent variables → variances add.
mistakes: Subtracting variances for a difference.
Not squaring the coefficients in the variance.
Using $\sigma$ instead of $\sigma/\sqrt n$ for a probability about $\bar X$.
Invoking a central limit theorem, which the supplied notes do not develop.
